review.headline: A dominant endgame slipped away into a theoretical draw

sections.text: You handled the Petrov's Defense smoothly, liquidating major pieces to reach an endgame where you took immediate control. When White slipped with 18.Bf4, you spotted the pin on the knight and struck with 18...Bxc3! to ruin their queenside structure. You activated your rook along the second rank with 20...Re2 and 21...Ra2, piling pressure onto their weak pawns.

White stumbled further in the endgame with 27.Bd6??, allowing you to capture a rook with 27...Nxc1! and emerge two pawns ahead. After 35.Kh4?? walked into a mating net, your 35...g5+! forced White's king into the corner. You were completely winning, but converting required patience rather than pawn trades.

With White's bishop locked down, your task was simply to push your passed b-pawn or maneuver your knight. Instead, 43...f5?? traded off pawns and allowed 44.gxf5+ Kxf5 45.Kh5, letting White eliminate your kingside pawns. Once White sacrificed their bishop for your last pawn with 48.Bxb4, you were left with a lone knight and no mating material.

review.turning_point: The win disappeared with 43...f5??, which opened the kingside and allowed White's king to eliminate your pawns, reducing the game to an unwinnable knight endgame.
review.focus: When ahead significant material in an endgame, avoid unnecessary pawn trades like 43...f5 that leave you with insufficient mating material.

review.headline: A sharp queenside counterattack undone by a final back-rank hallucination

sections.text: A symmetric opening quickly led to doubled pawns for you after White traded on f6. Instead of recapturing immediately, you opted for 5...Bxf3, pinning White's knight to the rook on h1 before the queens came off. After 7...gxf6 White jumped into d5 with 9.Nd5 and won a pawn with 10.Nxf6, leaving you playing catch-up in development.

You pushed on the queenside with 13...b5 and 14...b4, which lost another pawn but opened lines toward White's king. After doubling rooks on the b-file, you played 20...Bh6, establishing a pin along the c1-h6 diagonal against the f4 pawn. White erred with 21.Kd2, but you immediately sacrificed with 21...Nxb3+ 22.cxb3 Rxb3, giving up a piece for unclear compensation.

White stumbled right back with 23.Kc2, and you found the sharp 23...Rb2+! followed by 24...Bxf4+ to regain material and take control. However, on move 26, you went for a skewer on White's king and rook with 26...Rb1+, hoping for a decisive back rank attack, but forgot that the knight on c3 guarded b1. After 27.Nxb1, you resigned.

review.turning_point: After battling back into a winning position, 26...Rb1+ handed the game away by missing White's knight defense on the back rank.
review.focus: Always check all defender squares before forcing a tactical shot, as with 26...Rb1+ where 26...Rxg2 kept a winning advantage.

review.headline: A quick timeout victory after White seized the center

sections.text: You faced the Vienna Gambit with Black and chose a solid setup with 3...d6 and 4...Nbd7?!. While it kept your position intact, placing the knight on d7 blocked your light-squared bishop and gave White easy control over the central squares.

After both sides castled, White opened the center with 7.d4, and you traded pawns with 7...exd4. Kicking the knight with 8...c5?! gave White an easy retreat and weakened your d6-pawn, creating long-term structural targets.

The critical mistake came with 9...b6?, which was too slow. You needed active piece play like 9...Nb6 10.Bd3 to challenge White's active bishop. Instead, 9...b6 allowed White to strike immediately with 10.e5, forcing your knight backwards after 10...dxe5 11.fxe5 11...Ne8. However, the game concluded right here when White ran out of time.

review.turning_point: White cracked open your position with 10.e5 after your slow 9...b6, seizing a commanding space advantage before flagging.
review.focus: Prioritize active piece development and central counterplay over slow flank moves like 9...b6 when facing an opponent with central space.

review.headline: A wild rook endgame decided by a runaway passed pawn

sections.text: The game opened symmetrically in the French Variation of the Sicilian. After 4.e5 Ne4, you traded minor pieces steadily, eventually swapping queens with 17.Qxd7+ Kxd7. By move 20, you had reached a pure rook endgame, but Black gained the upper hand when you lost a pawn to 23...Rxe5.

Down a pawn, you had to defend passively while Black's rook roamed your territory. The position became chaotic around move 37. After your 37.g4, Black inexplicably blundered with 37...e5, hanging their rook on f5. You missed 38.gxf5 and played 38.Ke3 instead, but you quickly activated your rook with 39.Rb1! to stay in the fight.

After further pawn trades, you entered a race with your outside a-pawn against Black's f-pawn. Black slipped with 61...f4, and while you missed a back rank mate idea with 63.Rd8+ Kg8, Black stumbled again on 64...Ra8. You seized the chance with 65.a7!, cutting off the defense and queuing up 68.axb8=Q#.

review.turning_point: Black's 64...Ra8 walked into 65.a7!, which allowed your rook to invade the 7th and 8th ranks and force checkmate.
review.focus: Stay alert for free material when opponents get distracted: on move 38, 38.gxf5 would have simply won Black's rook.
